pumac-2012-power-01a.title: Triangle inequality
pumac-2012-power-01a.body:
Let $d=\deg f$, $M=\max(1,|\alpha|)$. For $0\le j\le d$ we have $|\alpha|^j\le M^j\le M^d$ (as $M\ge1$) and $|a_j|\le\lVert f\rVert$. Hence
$$|f(\alpha)|\le\sum_{j=0}^d|a_j||\alpha|^j\le\sum_{j=0}^d\lVert f\rVert M^d=(d+1)\lVert f\rVert M^d.\ \blacksquare$$

pumac-2012-power-01b.title: Coefficientwise
pumac-2012-power-01b.body:
Write $f=\sum a_jX^j$, $g=\sum b_jX^j$ (pad with zero coefficients). The $X^j$ coefficient of $\alpha f+\beta g$ is $\alpha a_j+\beta b_j$ and
$$|\alpha a_j+\beta b_j|\le|\alpha||a_j|+|\beta||b_j|\le|\alpha|\lVert f\rVert+|\beta|\lVert g\rVert.$$
Taking the maximum over $j$ gives the claim. $\blacksquare$

pumac-2012-power-01c.title: Count terms in each coefficient
pumac-2012-power-01c.body: Let $f=\sum_{i=0}^m a_iX^i$, $g=\sum_j b_jX^j$. The coefficient of $X^k$ in $fg$ is $\sum_{i+j=k}a_ib_j$ where $i$ ranges over at most $0,1,\dots,m$, i.e. at most $m+1$ terms, and each term satisfies $|a_ib_j|\le\lVert f\rVert\lVert g\rVert$. So every coefficient has absolute value at most $(m+1)\lVert f\rVert\lVert g\rVert$. $\blacksquare$

pumac-2012-power-02.title: Power series for $g$
pumac-2012-power-02.body:
Let $m=\deg f$, $n=\deg g=m-r$, $K=\max(1,|\alpha|^{-1})$. As formal power series in $X$ (valid since $\alpha\ne0$),
$$\frac1{(X-\alpha)^r}=(-\alpha)^{-r}\Bigl(1-\frac X\alpha\Bigr)^{-r}=\sum_{j\ge0}s_jX^j,\qquad s_j=(-\alpha)^{-r}\binom{j+r-1}{j}\alpha^{-j}.$$
Since $g=f\cdot(X-\alpha)^{-r}$ exactly, the coefficient $g_k$ ($0\le k\le n$) equals $\sum_{i=0}^kf_is_{k-i}$.

For $0\le j\le n$ we have $r+j\le m$, so $|\alpha|^{-(r+j)}\le K^{r+j}\le K^m$, and $\binom{j+r-1}{j}\le2^{j+r-1}<2^m$. Hence $|s_j|<(2K)^m$.
Therefore $|g_k|\le(k+1)\lVert f\rVert\max_j|s_j|<(n+1)(2K)^m\lVert f\rVert$, which is the claim since $n+1=1+\deg g$ and $m=\deg f$. $\blacksquare$

pumac-2012-power-03a.title: Minimal remainder
pumac-2012-power-03a.body: Consider $S=\{f-qg: q\in\mathbb Q[X]\}$; it is nonempty ($q=0$). If $0\in S$ we are done ($r=0$). Otherwise pick $r=f-qg\in S$ of minimal degree and suppose $\deg r\ge\deg g$. Let $s=\deg r-\deg g\ge0$ and let $c$ be the ratio (leading coeff of $r$)/(leading coeff of $g$) $\in\mathbb Q$. Then $r-cX^sg=f-(q+cX^s)g\in S$ has degree $<\deg r$ (or is $0$), contradicting minimality (or $0\in S$). Hence $\deg r<\deg g$. $\blacksquare$

pumac-2012-power-03b.title: Same proof, then the factor theorem
pumac-2012-power-03b.body:
The proof in part (a) only uses addition, multiplication and division of coefficients (to form the ratio $c$), i.e. only that the coefficients lie in a field. $\mathbb C$ is a field, so the same argument works verbatim.

Now divide $f$ by $g=X-\alpha$: $f=(X-\alpha)q+r$ with $r=0$ or $\deg r<1$, i.e. $r$ is a constant. Evaluating at $X=\alpha$ gives $r=f(\alpha)$. So $f(\alpha)=0$ iff $r=0$ iff $f=(X-\alpha)q$. $\blacksquare$

pumac-2012-power-04a.title: Bound the binomial coefficients
pumac-2012-power-04a.body: $D_kf=\sum_{j=k}^d\binom jk a_jX^{j-k}$ and $\binom jk\le\sum_i\binom ji=2^j\le2^d$. So each coefficient has absolute value at most $2^d|a_j|\le2^d\lVert f\rVert$. $\blacksquare$

pumac-2012-power-04b.title: Check on monomials
pumac-2012-power-04b.body: $D_1(X^j)=jX^{j-1}$, so $D_1$ is ordinary differentiation (linear). Applying it $k$ times to $X^j$ gives $j(j-1)\cdots(j-k+1)X^{j-k}=k!\binom jkX^{j-k}$ (and $0$ if $k>j$). By linearity, $D_1^{(k)}f=\sum_j a_j\,k!\binom jkX^{j-k}=k!\,D_kf$. $\blacksquare$

pumac-2012-power-04c.title: Taylor expansion about $\alpha$
pumac-2012-power-04c.body:
Write $X=(X-\alpha)+\alpha$ and expand with the binomial theorem:
$$f(X)=\sum_ja_j\bigl((X-\alpha)+\alpha\bigr)^j=\sum_ja_j\sum_{i\le j}\binom ji\alpha^{j-i}(X-\alpha)^i=\sum_i\Bigl(\sum_j\binom ji a_j\alpha^{j-i}\Bigr)(X-\alpha)^i=\sum_iD_if(\alpha)(X-\alpha)^i.$$
If $D_if(\alpha)=0$ for $0\le i<k$, then $f=(X-\alpha)^k\sum_{i\ge k}D_if(\alpha)(X-\alpha)^{i-k}$, so $(X-\alpha)^k$ divides $f$: the multiplicity of $\alpha$ is at least $k$. (If $f=0$ the claim is vacuous.) $\blacksquare$

pumac-2012-power-04c.title: Via the product rule
pumac-2012-power-04c.body: Induct on $k$. For $k=1$ the hypothesis $f(\alpha)=0$ gives $f=(X-\alpha)g$ (Problem 2.3). If $f=(X-\alpha)^{k-1}g$ and $f^{(i)}(\alpha)=0$ for $i<k$, then by Leibniz $f^{(k-1)}(\alpha)=(k-1)!\,g(\alpha)+0$, so $g(\alpha)=0$ and $(X-\alpha)^k\mid f$. (Use $D_i=f^{(i)}/i!$, from part (b).) $\blacksquare$

pumac-2012-power-05a.title: Leading terms
pumac-2012-power-05a.body: Let $f=aX^m+\dots$, $g=bX^n+\dots$ with $ab\ne0$. If $m=n$ we are done, so suppose $m\ne n$; then $m+n\ge1$. The coefficient of $X^{m+n-1}$ in $fDg$ is $nab$ and in $gDf$ it is $mab$, so $fDg=gDf$ forces $(n-m)ab=0$, i.e. $m=n$, a contradiction. $\blacksquare$

pumac-2012-power-05b.title: Cancel the leading term
pumac-2012-power-05b.body:
By part (a) $\deg f=\deg g$; let $a,b$ be the leading coefficients and $h=f-\frac abg$. Using $D(\cdot)$ linear,
$$hDg-gDh=fDg-\tfrac abgDg-gDf+\tfrac abgDg=fDg-gDf=0.$$
If $h\ne0$, then $(h,g)$ is a pair of nonzero polynomials satisfying the same relation, so by part (a) $\deg h=\deg g$. But the leading terms of $f$ and $\frac abg$ cancel, so $\deg h<\deg g$ — contradiction. Hence $h=0$ and $f=\frac abg$. $\blacksquare$

pumac-2012-power-05b.title: Logarithmic derivative
pumac-2012-power-05b.body: Factor $f=A\prod(X-a_i)$, $g=B\prod(X-b_j)$. The relation says $Df/f=Dg/g$, i.e. $\sum\frac1{X-a_i}=\sum\frac1{X-b_j}$. Both sides blow up exactly at the roots; comparing the residue at each root shows every number occurs equally often among the $a_i$ and the $b_j$, so $f/g=A/B$. $\blacksquare$

pumac-2012-power-06a.title: Substitution in both directions
pumac-2012-power-06a.body: If $f\in\mathbb Q[X]$ is nonzero of degree $d=\deg\alpha$ with $f(\alpha)=0$, then $g(X)=f\bigl(\frac{X-b}a\bigr)\in\mathbb Q[X]$ is nonzero of degree $d$ and $g(\beta)=f(\alpha)=0$. So $\beta$ is algebraic and $\deg\beta\le\deg\alpha$. Since $\alpha=\frac1a\beta-\frac ba$ is of the same form, the same argument gives $\deg\alpha\le\deg\beta$. $\blacksquare$

pumac-2012-power-06b.title: Make the polynomial monic
pumac-2012-power-06b.body:
Let $\alpha$ be a root of $f=c_dX^d+\dots+c_0$ with $c_d\ne0$; multiplying by a common denominator we may assume $c_j\in\mathbb Z$ and $c_d>0$. Put $a=c_d$. Multiply $f(\alpha)=0$ by $c_d^{d-1}$:
$$(c_d\alpha)^d+c_{d-1}(c_d\alpha)^{d-1}+c_{d-2}c_d(c_d\alpha)^{d-2}+\dots+c_0c_d^{d-1}=0.$$
So $a\alpha$ is a root of the monic integer polynomial $X^d+c_{d-1}X^{d-1}+c_{d-2}c_dX^{d-2}+\dots+c_0c_d^{d-1}$. $\blacksquare$

pumac-2012-power-06c.title: Shift the polynomial
pumac-2012-power-06c.body: Let $f\in\mathbb Z[X]$ be monic with $f(\alpha)=0$. Then $g(X)=f(X-b)$ is monic with integer coefficients (expand $(X-b)^j$), and $g(\alpha+b)=f(\alpha)=0$. $\blacksquare$

pumac-2012-power-06d.title: Induction on $r$
pumac-2012-power-06d.body:
Write $f=X^d+c_{d-1}X^{d-1}+\dots+c_0$, so $\alpha^d=-\sum_{j<d}c_j\alpha^j$, and $|c_j|\le\lVert f\rVert$.

*Base.* $r=0$: $a_{0,0}=1$, $a_{0,j}=0$ otherwise; $|a_{0,j}|\le1=(1+\lVert f\rVert)^0$.

*Step.* Suppose $\alpha^{r-1}=\sum_{j<d}a_{r-1,j}\alpha^j$ with $|a_{r-1,j}|\le B:=(1+\lVert f\rVert)^{r-1}$. Multiply by $\alpha$ and replace $\alpha^d$:
$$\alpha^r=\sum_{j=1}^{d-1}a_{r-1,j-1}\alpha^j+a_{r-1,d-1}\alpha^d=\sum_{j=0}^{d-1}\bigl(a_{r-1,j-1}-a_{r-1,d-1}c_j\bigr)\alpha^j,$$
with $a_{r-1,-1}:=0$. So $a_{r,j}=a_{r-1,j-1}-a_{r-1,d-1}c_j\in\mathbb Z$ and $|a_{r,j}|\le B+B\lVert f\rVert=(1+\lVert f\rVert)^r$. $\blacksquare$

pumac-2012-power-07a.title: Contrapositive (Gauss's lemma)
pumac-2012-power-07a.body:
We show: if $f,g$ are both simple then $fg$ is simple. Write $f=\sum a_iX^i$, $g=\sum b_iX^i$. Let $p$ be any prime. Since $f$ is simple (and nonzero), not all $a_i$ are divisible by $p$; likewise for $g$. Let $j$ be the least index with $p
mid a_j$ and $k$ the least with $p
mid b_k$. The coefficient of $X^{j+k}$ in $fg$ is
$$a_jb_k+\sum_{i<j}a_ib_{j+k-i}+\sum_{i<k}a_{j+k-i}b_i,$$
and every term of the sums is divisible by $p$ (it contains $a_i$ with $i<j$ or $b_i$ with $i<k$), while $p
mid a_jb_k$. So $p$ does not divide all coefficients of $fg$. This holds for every prime $p$, so $fg
e0$ and no integer $a>1$ divides all its coefficients: $fg$ is simple. $ lacksquare$

pumac-2012-power-07b.title: Use the content
pumac-2012-power-07b.body:
If $g=0$ there is nothing to prove. Otherwise choose $D\in\mathbb Z^+$ with $Dg\in\mathbb Z[X]$ and let $c$ be the gcd of its coefficients; then $Dg=ch$ with $h\in\mathbb Z[X]$ simple, so $g=\frac rsh$ with $\frac rs=\frac cD$ in lowest terms, $r,s\in\mathbb Z^+$.
Then $s\,(fg)=r\,(fh)$. Here $fh$ is simple (product of simple polynomials), so the gcd of the coefficients of the right side is exactly $r$. The left side is $s$ times the integer polynomial $fg$, so all its coefficients are divisible by $s$; hence $s\mid r$. As $\gcd(r,s)=1$, $s=1$ and $g=rh\in\mathbb Z[X]$. $\blacksquare$

pumac-2012-power-07c.title: Rescale the factors
pumac-2012-power-07c.body: Suppose $F\in\mathbb Z[X]$ and $F=GH$ with $G,H\in\mathbb Q[X]$ nonconstant. Choose $D\in\mathbb Z^+$ with $DG\in\mathbb Z[X]$ and divide out the gcd $c$ of its coefficients: $DG=cG_1$ with $G_1\in\mathbb Z[X]$ simple, so $G=\frac cDG_1$. Put $H_1=\frac cDH\in\mathbb Q[X]$. Then $F=G_1H_1$ with $G_1$ simple and $G_1H_1=F\in\mathbb Z[X]$; by the previous part $H_1\in\mathbb Z[X]$. Now $F=G_1H_1$ is a factorisation into two nonconstant polynomials in $\mathbb Z[X]$ ($\deg G_1=\deg G$, $\deg H_1=\deg H$). So if no such integer factorisation exists, no rational factorisation exists. $\blacksquare$

pumac-2012-power-08a.title: Irreducible implies separable
pumac-2012-power-08a.body:
*$m_\alpha$ is irreducible in $\mathbb Q[X]$:* if $m_\alpha=uv$ with $u,v\in\mathbb Q[X]$ nonconstant, then $\alpha$ is a root of $u$ or $v$, which has smaller degree (and can be made monic), contradicting minimality.

Let $m=m_\alpha$ and $Dm$ its derivative. $Dm\ne0$ and $\deg Dm<\deg m$, so $m\nmid Dm$. A common divisor of $m$ and $Dm$ in $\mathbb Q[X]$ is therefore a unit, and by the Euclidean algorithm (Problem 2.3) there are $u,v\in\mathbb Q[X]$ with $um+vDm=1$. If $\beta$ were a root of $m$ of multiplicity $\ge2$, then $m=(X-\beta)^2g$, so $Dm(\beta)=0$ too, and evaluating at $\beta$ gives $0=1$. Hence all roots are simple. $\blacksquare$

pumac-2012-power-08b.title: Compare with $m_\beta$
pumac-2012-power-08b.body: Let $\beta$ be a root of $f$ (so $\beta$ is algebraic). Then $m_\beta\mid f$ in $\mathbb Q[X]$ and $\deg m_\beta\ge1$. Because $f$ does not factor into two nonconstant rational polynomials, $f=c\,m_\beta$ with $c\in\mathbb Q^\times$. So $\deg\beta=\deg m_\beta=\deg f$, and the roots of $f$ are those of $m_\beta$, which are pairwise distinct by part (a). $\blacksquare$

pumac-2012-power-08c.title: Induction on $m$
pumac-2012-power-08c.body:
For $m=0$ the claim is trivial. If $m\ge1$, then $m_\alpha\mid f$, say $f=m_\alpha g$ with $g\in\mathbb Q[X]$ nonzero. Since $\alpha$ is a simple root of $m_\alpha$, it has multiplicity exactly $m-1$ in $g$. By induction $\deg g\ge(m-1)\deg\alpha$, so
$$\deg f=\deg m_\alpha+\deg g\ge\deg\alpha+(m-1)\deg\alpha=m\deg\alpha.\ \blacksquare$$

pumac-2012-power-08d.title: Divide by $(qX-p)^m$
pumac-2012-power-08d.body:
Dividing repeatedly by $X-p/q$ in $\mathbb Q[X]$ (remainder $0$ each time since $p/q$ is a root, Problem 2.3), $f=(X-\tfrac pq)^mg_0$ with $g_0\in\mathbb Q[X]$, hence $f=(qX-p)^mg$ with $g=q^{-m}g_0\in\mathbb Q[X]$.

The polynomial $F=(qX-p)^m$ has leading coefficient $q^m$ and constant term $(-p)^m$, which are coprime because $\gcd(p,q)=1$; so no integer $>1$ divides all coefficients and $F$ is simple. As $Fg=f\in\mathbb Z[X]$, we get $g\in\mathbb Z[X]$. Comparing leading coefficients, $a=q^m\cdot\mathrm{lc}(g)$ with $\mathrm{lc}(g)\in\mathbb Z\setminus\{0\}$. Hence $q^m\mid a$ and $q^m\le|a|$. $\blacksquare$

pumac-2012-power-08e.title: Gauss's lemma argument
pumac-2012-power-08e.body:
Let $f\in\mathbb Z[X]$ be monic with $f(\alpha)=0$. Then $m_\alpha\mid f$: $f=m_\alpha g$ with $g\in\mathbb Q[X]$ (monic). Pick $D\in\mathbb Z^+$ with $Dm_\alpha\in\mathbb Z[X]$, divide by the gcd $c$ of its coefficients, and put $A=\frac Dc m_\alpha=:a\,m_\alpha\in\mathbb Z[X]$, which is simple, with leading coefficient $a=\frac Dc>0$, so $a\in\mathbb Z^+$. Then
$$f=A\cdot\frac ga,\qquad A\text{ simple},\ \frac ga\in\mathbb Q[X],\ f\in\mathbb Z[X],$$
so $\frac ga\in\mathbb Z[X]$. Its leading coefficient is $\frac1a$ (as $g$ is monic), which is an integer; with $a\in\mathbb Z^+$ this forces $a=1$. Hence $m_\alpha=A\in\mathbb Z[X]$. $\blacksquare$

pumac-2012-power-09.title: Siegel's lemma via pigeonhole
pumac-2012-power-09.body:
Let $r=\lfloor(nA)^{m/(n-m)}\rfloor$. We assume $nA\ge1$ (automatic if some $a_{i,j}\ne0$, since $A\ge|a_{i,j}|\ge1$); then $r\ge1$.

Let $\beta_i=\sum_j\min(0,a_{i,j})$ and $\alpha_i=\sum_j\max(0,a_{i,j})$, so $\alpha_i-\beta_i=\sum_j|a_{i,j}|\le nA$. For $x\in\{0,1,\dots,r\}^n$ the integer $f_i(x)$ lies in $[\beta_ir,\alpha_ir]$, an interval with at most $r(\alpha_i-\beta_i)+1\le rnA+1$ integers. So $(f_1,\dots,f_m)$ takes at most $(rnA+1)^m$ values on the $(r+1)^n$ points of the box.

Since $r+1>(nA)^{m/(n-m)}$ we have $(r+1)^{n-m}>(nA)^m$, so
$$(r+1)^n=(r+1)^m(r+1)^{n-m}>\bigl((r+1)nA\bigr)^m\ge(rnA+1)^m,$$
using $nA\ge1$. By pigeonhole two distinct points $y\ne y'$ of the box have the same image. Then $x=y-y'\ne0$ satisfies $f_i(x)=0$ for all $i$ (linearity) and $|x_j|\le r$ for all $j$. $\blacksquare$

pumac-2012-power-10.title: Case by case
pumac-2012-power-10.body:
In all cases $|\alpha-p/q|<q^{-(1+\epsilon+d/2)}\le1/q$ for a solution $p/q$.

**$\alpha\notin\mathbb R$.** Then $|\alpha-p/q|\ge|\mathrm{Im}\,\alpha|>0$, so $q<1/|\mathrm{Im}\,\alpha|$; also $|p/q-\alpha|<1$ bounds $p$ for each $q$. Finitely many solutions.

**$d=1$.** $\alpha=a/b\in\mathbb Z/b$ in lowest terms. For $p/q\ne\alpha$: $|\alpha-p/q|=\frac{|aq-bp|}{bq}\ge\frac1{bq}$. A solution then needs $\frac1{bq}<q^{-3/2-\epsilon}$, i.e. $q^{1/2+\epsilon}<b$: $q$ is bounded, and $p$ is bounded for each $q$. Finitely many solutions (plus $p/q=\alpha$).

**$d=2$.** $\alpha$ is real, and $m_\alpha=(X-\alpha)(X-\alpha')\in\mathbb Z[X]$ with $\alpha'\in\mathbb R\setminus\{\alpha\}$ (real coefficients, simple roots). Both roots are irrational, so for $p/q$ in lowest terms $q^2m_\alpha(p/q)=p^2+apq+bq^2$ is a nonzero integer, i.e. $|m_\alpha(p/q)|\ge q^{-2}$. If $|\alpha-p/q|<1$ then $|\alpha'-p/q|\le1+|\alpha-\alpha'|$, so
$$\Bigl|\alpha-\frac pq\Bigr|=\frac{|m_\alpha(p/q)|}{|\alpha'-p/q|}\ge\frac1{(1+|\alpha-\alpha'|)q^2}.$$
A solution needs $\frac1{(1+|\alpha-\alpha'|)q^2}<q^{-2-\epsilon}$, i.e. $q^\epsilon<1+|\alpha-\alpha'|$: bounded $q$, hence finitely many solutions.

**$d\ge3$, $\alpha$ real.** Choose $n\in\mathbb Z$ with $\beta=\alpha+n\in I$. By Problem 3.1(a),(c), $\beta$ is an algebraic integer of the same degree $d$. Since $\bigl|\alpha-\frac pq\bigr|=\bigl|\beta-\frac{p+nq}q\bigr|$ and $\gcd(p+nq,q)=\gcd(p,q)=1$, $p/q\mapsto(p+nq)/q$ is a bijection between the solution sets for $\alpha$ and $\beta$, and the latter is finite by hypothesis. $\blacksquare$

pumac-2012-power-11.title: Linear equations and Siegel's lemma
pumac-2012-power-11.body:
**Setup.** By 3.3(e), $f=m_\alpha\in\mathbb Z[X]$ is monic of degree $d$; let $c_0=1+\lVert f\rVert\ge2$. By 3.1(d), $\alpha^r=\sum_{k<d}c_{r,k}\alpha^k$ with $c_{r,k}\in\mathbb Z$, $|c_{r,k}|\le c_0^r$. Note $0<\lambda<\tfrac12$ and $md<2n+2$.

**Equations.** Write $P=\sum_{i\le n}a_iX^i$, $Q=\sum_{i\le n}b_iX^i$ with unknown integers $a_i,b_i$ ($2n+2$ unknowns). Since $D_j$ is linear, condition (3) reads, for $0\le j<m$,
$$\sum_{i=j}^n\binom ij\bigl(a_i\alpha^{i-j}+b_i\alpha^{i-j+1}\bigr)=\sum_{k=0}^{d-1}\alpha^k\sum_{i=j}^n\binom ij\bigl(c_{i-j,k}a_i+c_{i-j+1,k}b_i\bigr)=0.$$
Because $\deg\alpha=d$, the numbers $1,\alpha,\dots,\alpha^{d-1}$ are linearly independent over $\mathbb Q$; so it suffices that every bracket vanishes. This is a system of $md$ homogeneous linear equations in the $2n+2$ unknowns with integer coefficients of absolute value at most $A:=2^nc_0^{n+1}$.

**Siegel's lemma.** As $2n+2>md$, Problem 3.4 gives a nonzero integer solution with
$$|a_i|,|b_i|\le\bigl((2n+2)A\bigr)^{\frac{md}{2n+2-md}}.$$
Now $2n+2-md=(2n+2)\lambda$, so the exponent is $\frac{1-\lambda}\lambda<\frac1\lambda$, and $(2n+2)A\le2^{n+1}2^nc_0^{n+1}\le(4c_0)^{2n}$ (for $n\ge1$). So (2) holds with $c_1=16c_0^2$, which depends only on $\alpha$; (1) and (3) hold by construction.

**(4).** First, $Q\ne0$: if $Q=0$ then $P\ne0$ and $D_jP(\alpha)=0$ for $j<m$, so by 2.4(c) $\alpha$ is a root of $P$ of multiplicity $\ge m$, and by 3.3(c) $n\ge\deg P\ge md>n+1$ (as $\frac{md}{n+1}>1$), a contradiction. Next suppose $P=cQ$ with $c\in\mathbb Q$ (this includes $P=0$). Then $0=D_j(P+\alpha Q)(\alpha)=(c+\alpha)D_jQ(\alpha)$ and $c+\alpha\ne0$ ($\alpha$ is irrational since $d\ge3$), so $D_jQ(\alpha)=0$ for $j<m$; as before $n\ge\deg Q\ge md>n+1$, a contradiction. $\blacksquare$

pumac-2012-power-12.title: Split and estimate
pumac-2012-power-12.body:
Note $D_jf=f^{(j)}/j!$ (Problem 2.4(b)) and $0<|\alpha|\le\frac12$ ($\alpha$ irrational).

**Divisibility.** By 2.4(c), $(X-\alpha)^m\mid P+\alpha Q$. Differentiating $j$ times (Leibniz), $G_j:=D_j(P+\alpha Q)$ is divisible by $(X-\alpha)^{m-j}$: $G_j=(X-\alpha)^{m-j}S_j$ with $S_j\in\mathbb C[X]$, $\deg S_j\le n$.

**Size of $S_j$.** By 2.4(a) and 2.1(b), $\lVert G_j\rVert\le\lVert D_jP\rVert+|\alpha|\lVert D_jQ\rVert\le2^n\cdot\tfrac32c_1^{n/\lambda}\le2^{n+1}c_1^{n/\lambda}$. If $S_j\ne0$, Problem 2.2 (with $r=m-j\ge1$, $\alpha\ne0$, $\max(1,|\alpha|^{-1})=|\alpha|^{-1}$) gives
$$\lVert S_j\rVert<(n+1)\Bigl(\frac2{|\alpha|}\Bigr)^{n}\lVert G_j\rVert\le2^n\cdot\Bigl(\frac2{|\alpha|}\Bigr)^n2^{n+1}c_1^{n/\lambda}\le\Bigl(\frac{16}{|\alpha|}\Bigr)^nc_1^{n/\lambda}\le\Bigl(\frac{16c_1}{|\alpha|}\Bigr)^{n/\lambda}.$$

**Evaluate.** Since $|\alpha-u|<q^{-\mu}<\tfrac12$ we get $|u|<1$. Now
$$D_j(P+vQ)(u)=G_j(u)+(v-\alpha)D_jQ(u)=(u-\alpha)^{m-j}S_j(u)+(v-\alpha)D_jQ(u).$$
By 2.1(a) (with $|u|<1$), $|S_j(u)|\le(n+1)\lVert S_j\rVert$ and $|D_jQ(u)|\le(n+1)\lVert D_jQ\rVert\le(n+1)2^nc_1^{n/\lambda}$. Therefore
$$|D_j(P+vQ)(u)|\le q^{-\mu(m-j)}(n+1)\Bigl(\frac{16c_1}{|\alpha|}\Bigr)^{n/\lambda}+s^{-\mu}(n+1)2^nc_1^{n/\lambda}.$$
With $n+1\le2^n\le2^{n/\lambda}$, both terms are at most $\bigl(\frac{32c_1}{|\alpha|}\bigr)^{n/\lambda}$ times the respective power of $q,s$. So the claim holds with $c_2=32c_1/|\alpha|$, which depends only on $\alpha$. $\blacksquare$

pumac-2012-power-13.title: Wronskian argument
pumac-2012-power-13.body:
**Nonvanishing.** By Problem 4.2(4), $P\ne0$, $Q\ne0$ and $P,Q$ are not proportional; so $P+vQ\ne0$ and $W:=Q\,DP-P\,DQ\ne0$ (otherwise $PDQ=QDP$ and Problem 2.5 would make $P,Q$ proportional). Also $W\in\mathbb Z[X]$. Since $P+vQ\ne0$, some $D_h(P+vQ)(u)$ is nonzero (Taylor expansion at $u$, Problem 2.4(c)); let $h\ge0$ be the least such index.

**$W$ vanishes to high order at $u$.** For $0\le i<h$: $D_iP(u)=-vD_iQ(u)$. Hence for $0\le i,j<h$,
$$D_iP(u)D_jQ(u)-D_jP(u)D_iQ(u)=-vD_iQ(u)D_jQ(u)+vD_jQ(u)D_iQ(u)=0.$$
By Leibniz, $W^{(k)}=\sum_{i=0}^k\binom ki\bigl(P^{(i+1)}Q^{(k-i)}-Q^{(i+1)}P^{(k-i)}\bigr)$ and $P^{(i)}=i!D_iP$. For $0\le k\le h-2$ every index $i+1$ and $k-i$ is $<h$, so every term vanishes at $u$: $D_kW(u)=0$ for $0\le k\le h-2$. By 2.4(c), $u$ is a root of $W$ of multiplicity $\ge h-1$.

**Size.** By Problem 3.3(d), $q^{h-1}\le|{\rm lc}(W)|\le\lVert W\rVert$. By 2.1(c) and 2.4(a),
$$\lVert W\rVert\le2(n+1)\cdot2^n\lVert P\rVert\lVert Q\rVert\le2^{2n+1}c_1^{2n/\lambda}\le(8c_1^2)^{n/\lambda}.$$
Taking logs, $(h-1)\log q\le\frac n\lambda\log(8c_1^2)$, i.e. $h\le1+\frac{c_3}\lambda\cdot\frac n{\log q}$ with $c_3=\log(8c_1^2)$. (If $h=0$ the bound is trivial.) $\blacksquare$

pumac-2012-power-14.title: Reductions, parameters, contradiction
pumac-2012-power-14.body:
**Reduction to algebraic integers.** Let $\alpha$ be algebraic of degree $d$. By 3.1(a),(b) there is $a\in\mathbb Z^+$ with $\beta=a\alpha$ an algebraic integer of degree $d$. Suppose $\alpha$ has infinitely many solutions $p/q$. Write $ap/q=p'/q'$ in lowest terms; then $q'\ge q/a$, the map $p/q\mapsto p'/q'$ is injective, and $q\ge q'$, so
$$\Bigl|\beta-\frac{p'}{q'}\Bigr|=a\Bigl|\alpha-\frac pq\Bigr|<a\,q^{-\mu}\le a\,q'^{-(1+\epsilon+d/2)}<q'^{-(1+\epsilon/2+d/2)}$$
whenever $q'^{\epsilon/2}>a$. Since for infinitely many distinct solutions $q$ (hence $q'\ge q/a$) is unbounded, $\beta$ has infinitely many solutions for the exponent $\epsilon/2\in(0,\frac12)$. So it suffices to prove the theorem for algebraic integers (for every $\epsilon$). By Problem 4.1 it suffices to treat algebraic integers $\alpha\in I=[-\frac12,\frac12]$ of degree $d\ge3$.

**Parameters.** Assume such an $\alpha$ has infinitely many solutions (for some $\epsilon\in(0,\frac12)$). Fix an even integer $t>4d/\epsilon-2$ and put $\lambda=\frac2{t+2}<\frac\epsilon{2d}$ (so $\lambda<\frac1{12}$), $\mu=1+\epsilon+\frac d2$. For $i\in\mathbb Z^+$ let
$$n+1=i\bigl(\tfrac t2+1\bigr)d,\qquad m=it,\qquad\text{so}\qquad\frac{md}{n+1}=2(1-\lambda)\in(1,2),\qquad 1-\frac{md}{2n+2}=\lambda.$$
Let $c_1,c_2,c_3$ be the constants of 4.2–4.4 (depending only on $\alpha$) and put $\delta=(1+\frac{2\epsilon}d)(1-\lambda)-1$. Since $\frac{2\epsilon}d<\frac13$, $\lambda(1+\frac{2\epsilon}d)<\frac{2\epsilon}{3d}$, so $\delta>\frac{4\epsilon}{3d}>\delta_0:=\frac\epsilon d$. Also $(\mu-1)m=(\epsilon+\frac d2)\frac{(2n+2)(1-\lambda)}d=(n+1)(1+\delta)$, hence
$$(\mu-1)m-n=\delta(n+1)+1>\delta_0n.\tag{1}$$

**Choosing $u,v$.** Infinitely many solutions force unbounded denominators. Put $L=\max\Bigl\{\dfrac{2(\log c_2+(\mu-1)c_3)}{\lambda\delta_0},\ \dfrac{c_3d}\lambda,\ \log 2\Bigr\}$ and fix $i_0$ with $n_0=i_0(\frac t2+1)d-1\ge\max\{2d,\ 2(t+\mu)/\delta_0\}$. Choose a solution $u=p/q$ with $\log q>L$, then a solution $v=r/s$ so far out that $x:=\frac{\log s}{\log q}>t(i_0+1)$ (in particular $s>q$). The interval $[x-t,x)$ contains exactly one multiple $m=it$ of $t$; then $i\ge i_0$, so $n\ge n_0$. Fix $n$ accordingly, and $P,Q$ from 4.2. We have
$$q^m<s\le q^{m+t}.\tag{2}$$

**The index $h$.** Let $h$ be as in 4.4: $D_h(P+vQ)(u)=:w\ne0$ and $h\le1+\frac{c_3n}{\lambda\log q}$. Since $\log q>c_3d/\lambda$, $h\le1+\frac nd<m$ (using $m=\frac{(2n+2)(1-\lambda)}d>\frac{11}{6}\cdot\frac{n+1}d$ and $n\ge2d$), so Problem 4.3 applies with $j=h$.

**Lower bound.** $D_hP,D_hQ\in\mathbb Z[X]$ have degree $\le n-h$ and $v=r/s$, hence $q^{n-h}s\,w\in\mathbb Z\setminus\{0\}$ and $|w|\ge\dfrac1{q^{n-h}s}$.

**Upper bound.** By 4.3 and $s>q^m\ge q^{m-h}$: $|w|\le c_2^{n/\lambda}(q^{-\mu(m-h)}+s^{-\mu})\le2c_2^{n/\lambda}q^{-\mu(m-h)}$.

**Comparison.** Together, $q^{\mu(m-h)}\le2c_2^{n/\lambda}q^{n-h}s$. Take $\log$, divide by $\log q$ and use $\log s\le(m+t)\log q$ from (2):
$$\mu(m-h)\le n-h+m+t+\frac{\log2+\frac n\lambda\log c_2}{\log q},\quad\text{i.e.}\quad(\mu-1)m-n\le t+(\mu-1)h+\frac{\log2+\frac n\lambda\log c_2}{\log q}.$$
Insert $h\le1+\frac{c_3n}{\lambda\log q}$ and (1):
$$\delta_0n<t+(\mu-1)+\frac{\log2}{\log q}+\frac{n}{\lambda\log q}\bigl(\log c_2+(\mu-1)c_3\bigr)<t+\mu+\frac{\delta_0}2n,$$
using $\log q>L$. So $n<\frac{2(t+\mu)}{\delta_0}\le n_0\le n$, a contradiction. Hence there are only finitely many solutions. $\blacksquare$
